### Questions people ask before we talk

What kind of businesses do you work with?Small and mid-sized businesses in Hamilton, the GTA and across Ontario. Machine shops and plants with industrial IT, contractors with no in-house IT, and service businesses that want AI that answers customers without inventing things.

Can you take over infrastructure someone else installed?That is most of the work. I document what is there, find what is fragile, and fix the parts that will cost you a weekend. Nothing gets ripped out to make room for a preferred brand.

Do you build AI that runs in production, or prototypes?Production. Validation gates before a model output reaches a customer, logging so every conversation is replayable, and monitoring so you hear about problems before your customers do. I have run over 500,000 validated AI interactions across production pipelines.

Are you taking contract work, or a full time role?Both. Cloud and Cable is the delivery business for client work, and I am open to senior in-house roles in Canada, remote, the United States or Europe.

## AI for small business: start with the boring stuff | Stefan Yasin

URL: https://stefanyasin.com/blog/ai-for-small-business/

Writing (/blog/) / EssayOctober 21, 2026· AI

## AI for small business: start with the boring stuff

The unglamorous automations pay first. The chatbots come later.

Every small business owner has now seen the AI demo: the chatbot, the image generator, the assistant that writes emails. And most of them have also felt the letdown when the demo did not survive contact with their actual Tuesday.

Here is the order that actually pays, built from watching it work and watching it fail.

First: document and inbox automation. Invoices, intake forms, booking requests, and the repetitive emails that eat two hours a day. This is where the hours are, and the risk is near zero. If the automation gets something wrong, a human sees it in minutes.

Second: meeting notes and summaries. Transcription pipelines that turn a consultation into a clean summary and action list. Small businesses live and die on follow-up, and follow-up dies when notes live in a notebook nobody reopens.

Third: internal tools. Quote generators, triage forms, and the small apps that turn a twenty-minute manual task into a two-minute one. Built around the actual workflow, not the vendor’s template.

Only then: the customer-facing chatbot. By this point you have the content and the processes to feed it, which is what makes the difference between a chatbot that answers and a chatbot that apologizes.

The pattern underneath all of it: AI that pays for itself in hours, deployed where a human still catches the mistakes. Glamour is a marketing problem. Time is a business problem.

Written by Stefan Yasin, Hamilton, Ontario.

## Backups are a promise you have not tested | Stefan Yasin

URL: https://stefanyasin.com/blog/backups-are-a-promise-untested/

Writing (/blog/) / EssayOctober 22, 2026· Operations

## Backups are a promise you have not tested

A backup you have never restored is a hope, not a plan. Test it before the bad day decides for you.

I have watched two businesses learn the same lesson in the same week. Both had backups. One had tested them.

The first owner showed me a shelf of drives and a cloud dashboard full of green checkmarks. The backup software had reported success every night for two years. When the server died, we discovered the drives had been unreadable for months, because the software had been backing up to a folder on the same machine that failed. The green checkmarks were measuring effort, not results.

The second owner had a simpler setup and a weirder habit: once a quarter, he wiped a spare machine and restored everything onto it. It took him an afternoon. When his machine died, he was back at work the next morning, mildly annoyed instead of destroyed.

The difference was not money. It was one question: has anyone ever restored this backup and opened the files?

Backups fail two ways. The first is silent: a job stops running, a drive fills, a path changes, and every report keeps saying success. The second is at the moment of truth: the backup runs fine, but the restore was never practiced, so nobody knows the steps, the password, or the order. Both are fixed by the same boring habit: a scheduled restore drill.

The drill does not need to be heroic. Once a quarter, restore to a spare machine or a test folder. Open the files. Time it. Write down the steps, because the day you need them is not the day to learn them. Keep one copy offsite and one offline, because ransomware targets the backup too, and a backup on the same network is a hostage, not a rescue.

I built a small tool that automates the verification for GitHub-based backups, checking that a restore actually works and cleaning up after itself. It is open source at github.com/StefanYasin/restore-drill (https://github.com/StefanYasin/restore-drill). The tool matters less than the habit it enforces.

If you cannot say “we restored from backup last month and it worked,” you do not have a backup plan. You have a promise. Promises are cheap until the invoice lands.

This is the first question we ask every Cloud and Cable client, before we touch a cable: show me a restore that worked.

Written by Stefan Yasin, Hamilton, Ontario.

## The first 90 days of AI in a small business | Stefan Yasin

URL: https://stefanyasin.com/blog/first-90-days-ai-small-business/

Writing (/blog/) / EssayOctober 22, 2026· AI

## The first 90 days of AI in a small business

A calendar, not a demo. Three months of boring automations that pay for themselves before the chatbots arrive.

I keep hearing the same story: a business buys an AI chatbot, points it at their website, and waits for the savings. Six months later the chatbot is still answering “what are your hours” and the owner has decided AI was hype.

AI was not the problem. The order was.

Small businesses do not need intelligence first. They need their repetitive work to stop eating their week. The first 90 days of AI should be a calendar, not a demo.

Month one: paper and inbox. Point an automation at the boring intake work. Receipts, invoices, emails that ask the same three questions, documents that need filing under a name and a date. This is not glamorous. It pays immediately, because it removes the work nobody wants to do and everyone does badly at 4pm on a Friday.

Month two: first drafts, human review. Draft the responses, the quotes, the FAQ answers, the meeting summaries. A human reads and sends every one. You are buying time on the thinking part, not the judgment part. The moment you skip the review, the savings stop being savings.

Month three: the digest. One automated report a week: what arrived, what was paid, what has not been answered, what is trending wrong. Now the AI is not doing a task. It is giving the owner their week back in one page.

What to skip until this works: chatbots on the website, agents with access to your accounts, anything that promises to run your business. Those are month ten tools wearing month one clothes. If the boring automations did not pay, the clever ones will not either.

The test is money. At day 90, ask one question: what did this replace? If the answer is “a demo,” start again with the receipts.

This is the same playbook I wrote about in AI for small business: start with the boring stuff (/blog/ai-for-small-business/), and it is the one we run at Cloud and Cable. The bots come later. The boring stuff pays first.

Written by Stefan Yasin, Hamilton, Ontario.

## What plant IT taught me about small business | Stefan Yasin

URL: https://stefanyasin.com/blog/plant-it-to-small-business/

Writing (/blog/) / EssayOctober 21, 2026· Operations

## What plant IT taught me about small business

Downtime is measured in dollars per minute in both places. The difference is who feels it.

I spent years running IT where a stopped line was a phone call you never wanted: plant floors, packaging lines, building systems that fed entire facilities. Then I started working with small business, and everyone assumed the stakes were lower.

They are not. The numbers are smaller and the impact is closer.

When a press stops, the company loses production by the minute. When a small office loses its server, the owner loses the weekend, the payroll run, and a piece of their relationship with every client who could not reach them. Both are downtime. One just fits on a spreadsheet.

The lesson that transfers: boring is the goal. In a plant, nobody wants excitement from the SCADA system. Small business deserves the same standard: backups that have been tested, cabling that is labelled, documentation that survives the person who built it, and monitoring that pages you before the client notices.

The second lesson: the person who understands the whole stack wins. In industrial environments, the best troubleshooters knew the mechanical, the electrical, and the controls layer. Small business has the same shape: the machine, the network, the cloud subscription, and the AI tooling that now sits on top. A provider who only knows one layer is a pass-through. The value is in owning the whole chain.

That is why Cloud and Cable exists: plant-floor standards, applied to the businesses that never thought they could afford them.

Written by Stefan Yasin, Hamilton, Ontario.

## The Real Ops Stack Nobody Talks About | Stefan Yasin

URL: https://stefanyasin.com/blog/the-real-ops-stack-nobody-talks-about/

Writing (/blog/) / EssayNovember 7, 2026· Operations

## The Real Ops Stack Nobody Talks About

The ops stack nobody talks about. Why cross-domain depth across plant systems, BMS networking, IT, and AI pipelines beats single-silo management.

Most IT leadership job postings still read like carbon copies from 2012. They ask for eight to ten years of progressive experience inside a single corporate silo. You manage the help desk, you move up to systems administration, and eventually you get a director title.

That progression makes sense on a recruiter checklist. In the real world, it leaves massive blind spots.

Real operations in 2026 doesn’t stay inside neat departmental boxes. It spans enterprise networks, industrial machinery, building automation, vendor contracts, and automated AI pipelines. If you’ve only worked behind a clean office desk, half of your operational surface is completely invisible to you. Cross-domain depth across those boundaries is far more valuable than a decade spent managing the exact same ticket queue.

Here are three real examples of cross-domain operations that delivered results traditional IT managers would’ve missed entirely.

First: connecting plant building automation into enterprise monitoring.

In most facilities, building management systems (BMS) operate on an island. Chillers, air compressors, backup generators, and power distribution panels run on isolated fieldbuses like BACnet or Modbus. Traditional IT managers treat building controls as facilities work, completely separate from their domain.

That wall causes outages. When an HVAC compressor stalls on a humid summer afternoon, your server room doesn’t care about organizational charts. The temperature spikes, switches throttle, and hardware shuts down on thermal protection.

By bridging BMS controllers into standard enterprise monitoring using SNMP and time-series collectors, you see the warning signs early. You track compressor duty cycles, fan currents, and ambient intake temperatures alongside CPU utilization. You catch electrical drops and cooling failures hours before an expensive breaker trips. The physical facility and the server rack are the exact same system.

Second: applying AI automation to internal service workflows instead of public chat.

Every vendor wants to sell you a customer-facing conversational bot. Most of them turn into expensive toys that frustrate users and generate apologies.

The real return on investment sits on the internal side of operations. Across more than 500,000 production AI interactions, the highest-value automations are never flashy. They handle event classification, vendor notification parsing, and incident triage.

When a network monitoring probe reports an interface flap, an automated pipeline can parse the raw alert, correlate it against recent switch configuration logs, and draft the remediation ticket with full diagnostics attached. The on-call engineer gets a validated problem summary instead of thirty fragmented alert emails. You cut mean time to resolution from forty-five minutes down to four, without putting an unvetted chatbot in front of clients.

Third: treating shadow IT as a product problem rather than a policy violation.

Traditional IT management responds to shadow IT with policy memos and firewall blocks. When an engineering team signs up for an external cloud tool or marketing runs data through a new SaaS platform, IT leadership calls it a compliance breach.

That response misses the point. Employees adopt outside tools because internal systems failed to deliver the workflow they need to do their jobs. Shadow IT isn’t a discipline problem. It’s product telemetry telling you where your internal stack is broken.

When you treat user workarounds as user research, your governance model shifts. You don’t issue reprimands. You wrap the outside tool in single sign-on, audit its data storage policies, monitor API spend, and integrate it safely into the core network. You protect the company while removing the friction that drove people away in the first place.

The next operations leader won’t come from people who stayed inside one safe lane for eight years. It’ll come from operators who have worked across enough domains to know what breaks, what matters, and what can be automated. When you understand the whole stack from the power panel to the model pipeline, you stop firefighting. Companies that recognize that cross-domain reality win.

Written by Stefan Yasin, Hamilton, Ontario.

## The two questions that stop most small business breaches | Stefan Yasin

URL: https://stefanyasin.com/blog/two-questions-stop-small-business-breaches/

Writing (/blog/) / EssayOctober 22, 2026· Security

## The two questions that stop most small business breaches

Stored credentials and untested backups cause more damage than exotic malware. Two boring questions fix most of it.

I recently ran an audit on a working machine, the kind a small business owner uses every day. The scan found over thirty stored credentials sitting in the operating system’s credential vault, including old ones for systems that no longer exist. Nothing exotic. Just years of “remember this password.”

Now imagine what an AI agent, or any tool with too much access, does when it finds thirty saved passwords. It does not need to be clever. It just needs to be running as you.

Small business breaches rarely come from exotic malware. They come from three boring things: credentials left lying around, backups that were never tested, and software that stopped getting patched because nobody owned the job. I wrote about the backups in backups are a promise you have not tested (/blog/backups-are-a-promise-untested/). This is the credentials part.

The first question: who can touch what? If an employee leaves, does every password they ever saw get changed? If a tool runs as the owner, can it reach the bank login? Most small businesses answer “probably” to both. Probably is how breaches happen.

The second question: do we know what is running? On the machine I audited, services were listening on the network that nobody had opened on purpose, and startup programs were running from folders any user could write to. Each one is a doorway with the door wedged open.

Neither question needs a security team. They need one boring audit and one boring habit. Review stored credentials quarterly and delete what you do not use. Turn on multi-factor authentication everywhere it exists, because a stolen password stops mattering when there is a second door. Patch on a schedule, not when you remember.

I put the audit into an open source tool, agent-surface-report (https://github.com/StefanYasin/agent-surface-report), on GitHub. It answers both questions in one pass and prints what to do about each finding.

The expensive breach is not the one in the news. It is the one your business absorbs quietly: the drained account, the locked files, the client who leaves. Two questions, asked quarterly, prevent most of them. Ask them before a tool asks them for you.

Written by Stefan Yasin, Hamilton, Ontario.

## What a small business should actually monitor | Stefan Yasin

URL: https://stefanyasin.com/blog/what-small-business-should-monitor/

Writing (/blog/) / EssayOctober 23, 2026· Operations

## What a small business should actually monitor

Five things, not five hundred. Monitoring works when it pages the right person about the right failure.

Every monitoring dashboard a small business buys starts the same way: five hundred widgets, all green, nobody watching. Then the server dies on a Saturday and the owner finds out from a client.

Monitoring is not about seeing everything. It is about deciding what deserves to interrupt someone, and who that someone is.

I learned this in a plant, the expensive way. We watched everything: network gear, servers, building systems, production equipment. Everything pinged everyone, so nothing mattered to anyone. An alert with no owner is a dashboard, not an alert. The fix was not more tools. It was five categories and one named owner per category.

For a small business, the five things that actually matter:

- Backup age, not backup status. How old is the newest good copy? If that number grows, something quietly stopped working.

- Disk health and space. Drives fail slowly before they fail fast. The slow part gives you weeks.

- Power. A UPS on battery is a countdown. Knowing the minute it starts is the difference between a clean shutdown and a scramble.

- Reachability from outside. A ping from inside the network proves nothing. The question is whether a client can reach you right now.

- The heartbeat. Something outside your building should notice if your building goes quiet. If your monitoring lives on the server it watches, silence looks exactly like health.

And the rule that makes it stick: every alert has one owner. If nobody can say “I get woken up for this,” it is not an alert, it is decoration.

This is the same model I run for my own fleet of automation agents, with a dashboard called agentpulse (https://github.com/StefanYasin/agentpulse), and it is the first thing we install at Cloud and Cable. Five things, one owner each, and an inbox that stays quiet until something real happens.

Written by Stefan Yasin, Hamilton, Ontario.

## About | Stefan Yasin

URL: https://stefanyasin.com/about/

## Operator. Builder. Straight answers.

I have spent a decade where downtime is expensive: plant floors, data closets, server rooms, and the networks between them. That background shapes everything I build now, from Cloud and Cable's infrastructure practice to the AI systems I run for small business.

My rule for AI is the same as my rule for cabling: if you cannot explain what it does in one sentence, do not install it. Most small businesses do not need a chatbot. They need the boring automations, done correctly, that save ten hours a week.

### Industrial roots

Plant IT, networking, and building management systems. Decommissioned a Mississauga facility, commissioned a new one in North York.

### Infrastructure, end to end

Cabling, racks, servers, PLCs, SCADA, VMware, and the documentation that makes it all survive the person who built it.

### AI that ships

Automation pipelines and AI tooling running in production for real businesses. If it does not pay for itself, it does not get built.

### Hamilton, Ontario

Local operator with a global view. SMB AI adoption, open source tooling, and infrastructure done properly.

### Datacenter & electrical

Datacenter buildouts and decommissions, electrical and power systems, and the low-voltage work that connects them. Managed trades on site, not just from a desk.

### Cloud & AI architecture

Cloud migrations, SaaS stacks, and AI pipelines for small business, architected to pay for themselves.
